summary: Defines the revised IDNA protocol for registering and looking up internationalized domain names without changing the DNS itself. It is meant only for domain names, not free text. It is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 3490 and RFC 3491.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers only understand a simple alphabet for website names. This gives a trick for turning names in any language into that simple form, so the old system still works.

subtitle: The protocol that lets non-ASCII domain names work on today's DNS by encoding them as plain ASCII labels.

tldr.problem: People want domain names in their own scripts, but the existing DNS infrastructure only handles ASCII labels.
tldr.mechanism: Applications convert a non-ASCII label to an ASCII form using Punycode with the prefix xn--, after checking it against registration or lookup rules. Servers and resolvers need no change.
tldr.outcome: This is the IDNA2008 protocol. It obsoletes RFC 3490 and RFC 3491 and updates RFC 3492.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document is the protocol definition for Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA), in the version known as IDNA2008. Terminology and a road map to the other IDNA2008 documents are in a separate Definitions document (RFC 5890), and the reasons for the changes are in the Rationale document (RFC 5894).

IDNA lets applications use certain ASCII labels, beginning with a special prefix, to stand for non-ASCII labels. Lower layers need not know about this. IDNA does not require changes to DNS servers, resolvers or protocol elements, because the existing ASCII name service is used.

The document describes two separate protocols that share terminology and operations: one for registration and one for lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: The old phone book can only print simple letters. So names written in other alphabets get a secret code spelled with simple letters, and the phone book never needs to change.

sections.title: Core Requirements
sections.content:
IDNA makes three requirements. First, when a domain name goes into a slot that is not IDNA-aware, it MUST contain only ASCII characters, meaning its labels are A-labels or NR-LDH labels, unless the application is not bound by the historical hostname-style rules.

Second, labels MUST be compared in equivalent forms: both A-label or both U-label. Pairs of A-labels are compared as case-insensitive ASCII, as with all ASCII DNS labels. U-labels are compared as-is, without case folding. Comparing labels does not require validating them, but validation SHOULD be performed in many cases.

Third, labels being registered MUST follow the registration rules, and labels being looked up MUST follow the lookup rules.

An A-label is the ASCII form of an internationalized label, and a U-label is the Unicode form. They convert into each other without loss of information.
sections.plainLanguage: Every name has two spellings: the fancy one in its own alphabet and a plain coded one. When two names are compared, both must be in the same spelling.

sections.title: Where IDNA Applies
sections.content:
IDNA applies to all domain names in all domain name slots in protocols, except where explicitly excluded. It does not apply to slots that do not use the LDH syntax rules. In older protocols that are not IDNA-aware, internationalized names MUST stay in A-label form, and any IDN that appears in DNS queries or responses MUST be an A-label.

In DNS resource records, IDNA applies only to domain names in the NAME and RDATA fields of records whose CLASS is IN. It depends on the CLASS, not the TYPE, unless a new TYPE defines its own rules. Underscore labels, such as those used for SRV records, are incompatible with IDNA coding.

IDNA does not make other data stored in domain names international. The RFC's example is an email address local part held in the SOA RNAME field: existing email standards allow only ASCII there, and IDNA does not change them.
sections.plainLanguage: The coding trick is for names in the address book only. It does not change how other things, like the first half of an email address, are written.

sections.title: The Registration Protocol
sections.content:
By the time a string enters registration it MUST be Unicode in Normalization Form C (NFC). Registries MUST accept only the exact string requested, with no mappings or local adjustments. They MAY take it as an A-label and U-label pair, an A-label only, or a U-label only. The first two are recommended, and the pair is normally preferred because it lets the registry check user intent.

If both forms are supplied, the registry converts the A-label to a U-label, runs the tests on that U-label, and checks that the A-label it produces matches the one provided, rejecting the registration if anything differs. The tests are:

  • No characters from the DISALLOWED or UNASSIGNED lists in the Tables document (RFC 5892).
  • No -- in the third and fourth positions, and no leading or trailing hyphen.
  • No leading combining mark.
  • Any CONTEXTJ or CONTEXTO code point needs a defined contextual rule that passes.
  • Labels with right-to-left characters MUST meet the Bidi criteria (RFC 5893).

A string with at least one non-ASCII character that passes all tests and is 63 or fewer characters long in ASCII-compatible encoding (ACE) form is a U-label. Registries may also apply their own policies. Finally, the U-label is converted to an A-label by Punycode (RFC 3492) with the ACE prefix xn-- in front, and that A-label is inserted into the zone.
sections.plainLanguage: Registering a name is like a strict airport check. The registry looks closely at every letter, and only then writes the coded version in the phone book.

sections.title: The Lookup Protocol
sections.content:
Lookup is more permissive than registration because it assumes names present in the DNS are valid. The user supplies a string in a local character set, and the application converts it to Unicode in NFC form, which may involve mappings handled outside this document.

If the input already looks like an A-label (it starts with xn--, case-insensitively), the application MAY convert it to a U-label to check it, and if it does, it MUST reject the label if the result is not identical to the original. It SHOULD do the conversion if the name will be shown to the user in native characters.

Putative U-labels MUST be rejected before the DNS lookup if they are not in NFC, have -- in the third and fourth positions, begin with a combining mark, contain DISALLOWED or unassigned code points, or fail required contextual rules. Applications SHOULD also check the Bidi rules, which gives better error information. For all other strings the application MUST rely on the DNS to decide validity, and declining to look up a conforming string is not conformant. Valid labels are converted with Punycode and the xn-- prefix, then resolved with normal DNS procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: When you look a name up, the check is lighter. You only turn away names that are clearly broken, then turn the rest into the coded form and ask the phone book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document does not carry the main security discussion. It is in the Definitions document (RFC 5890), except for right-to-left scripts, which are covered in RFC 5893.

To avoid attacks from labels that can be confused with others, or from rendering problems, the IDNA model requires registries to be careful about which labels they permit. The RFC points to its section on registry restrictions and the Rationale document for a fuller discussion. It also says there are no IANA actions in the components described here, because those actions are in the Tables document.
sections.plainLanguage: Some letters look alike, so tricksters could fake a name. The people who hand out names are asked to be careful about which ones they allow.

sections.title: What Changed from IDNA2003
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the major changes from the earlier version, IDNA2003:

  • The character set is Unicode version agnostic instead of fixed at Unicode 3.2.
  • Registration and lookup are defined separately.
  • Symbol and punctuation characters are disallowed except for needed exceptions.
  • Mapping and normalization are removed from the protocol and done by applications beforehand.
  • Allowed characters follow Unicode properties plus a small human-made exclusion list.
  • Some characters are usable only in specific contexts.
  • Words in languages such as Dhivehi and Yiddish can be expressed.
  • Bidirectional names display in a less surprising way.
  • The dot separator is removed from the mandatory part of the protocol.
  • Some currently valid labels that are not actually IDNA labels become invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the list of fixes in the new rulebook compared with the old one: simpler rules, more languages, and less guessing about what a letter means.
